topics.title: 16.1.1 Separating Cached Copies from Authoritative State
topics.summary: A cache stores information that can be reconstructed under an explicit policy. If losing an entry loses the only record of a completed effect, that entry is authoritative state regardless of whether the code calls it a cache. HarborDispatch’s worker receipts are not expendable cache entries; they define how delayed retries are interpreted.

topics.summary: Freshness is a requirement, not a consequence of a fast lookup. Specify whether a value may be stale for a bounded duration, must meet a minimum revision, or is safe only for advisory display. Different fields on one page can have different requirements.

topics.title: 16.2.1 Rejecting Old Fills After an Invalidation
topics.summary: The model records a minimum acceptable version, called a floor, for each invalidated key. Invalidation at version 5 evicts an older cached value and prevents a later fill of version 4 from being inserted. A fill at version 5 or later remains eligible under the model’s rule.

topics.title: 16.2.2 Bounding the Metadata Needed to Reject Staleness
topics.summary: Remembering every invalidation forever would itself become unbounded storage. The teaching model keeps maps of entries and floors and deliberately does not implement eviction or floor garbage collection. Its purpose is to expose the correctness requirement before optimizing memory use.

topics.title: 16.3.1 Preventing Simultaneous Misses from Overloading the Authority
topics.summary: A popular entry expires and thousands of requests miss together. If each independently fetches from the database, the cache has concentrated load into a burst. Fill coalescing can allow one in-flight fetch per key while other callers wait or receive a defined stale result.

cards.answer: A popular entry expires and thousands of requests miss together. If each independently fetches from the database, the cache has concentrated load into a burst. Fill coalescing can allow one in-flight fetch per key while other callers wait or receive a defined stale result.

topics.title: Engineering case — Reclaim invalidation floors without reopening the race
topics.summary: The versioned cache stores a floor of 20 for key K. A read of version 19 began before invalidation and remains in flight. An eviction policy removes K’s floor to reclaim memory. The old read then completes and inserts version 19 because the cache no longer remembers that version 20 was required.

reading.title: Engineering case — Reclaim invalidation floors without reopening the race
paragraphs: The versioned cache stores a floor of 20 for key K. A read of version 19 began before invalidation and remains in flight. An eviction policy removes K’s floor to reclaim memory. The old read then completes and inserts version 19 because the cache no longer remembers that version 20 was required.

A bounded implementation needs more than a maximum map size. It needs a rule for when outstanding old fills can no longer publish. One approach assigns a cache generation to each fill. When a generation is retired, its fills may complete for their callers under a defined policy but cannot repopulate the new generation’s cache.

Another approach bounds fill lifetime and retains invalidation metadata until every fill that could predate it has completed or been invalidated. This requires tracking actual operation lifetime, not assuming that a timeout stopped a remote callback. The cancellation lessons from the coroutine chapter apply here too.

A generation reset can safely cause more misses, but it must not let untrusted or stale callbacks bypass the publication check. The callback should carry the generation captured at admission and compare it at publication under the same synchronization that protects cache state.

The model’s put method accepts equal versions and replaces the value. That assumes a version uniquely identifies the authoritative state for the key. If two different values can legitimately carry the same version, the protocol is underspecified. A production implementation may need to reject equal-version conflicts or compare an authoritative content identifier.

Test reclamation with an explicit delayed fill. Invalidate, retire the relevant generation, reclaim metadata, then deliver the old completion. The expected result is rejection of cache publication, not necessarily cancellation of every caller’s operation. These are separate outcomes.

This case reveals why cache metadata is not always disposable in the same way as cached payload. It can encode a temporal safety condition. A capacity optimization must preserve that condition or replace it with another mechanism whose assumptions are equally clear.
